full_text:
The 2026 NFL Draft recently concluded, and sportsbooks didn’t waste any time getting their initial rookie futures out to the betting public. It’s time to see who the best candidates are to bring home the awards for Offensive Rookie of the Year and Defensive Rookie of the Year. I gave out the 2024 OROY winner, __Jayden Daniels,__ at +1400 odds in this article two years ago, which netted us 7 units in profit.

Wagering your hard-earned money in May and waiting for bets to be settled next February isn’t the easiest pill to swallow. Nevertheless, if we can get the best of the lines before the markets fully mature, it makes the wait until the end of the season worth it in the long run. Shop around for the best lines and odds if you have access to multiple sportsbooks. You’ll see more volatility between books on NFL Futures in the off-season than you’ll see on game lines and player props during the season. Let’s see if we can find some value in these rookie player props.

\>Be sure to check out [Brolley’s Best Bets: 2026 NFL Futures](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/series/2026/best-bets) for my favorite futures bets all offseason…Subscribe to the Best Bets Podcast on your [favorite platform](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/podcasts/show/nfl-best-bets) and on [YouTube](https://www.youtube.com/@FantasyPointsBetting) for year-round NFL betting talk…Join our “#official-bets” [Fantasy Points Discord](https://www.fantasypoints.com/media/discord) to see our staff's wagers as soon as we make them!

__Rookie of the Year Winners from the Last Decade__
---------------------------------------------------

\>Historic odds courtesy of [SportsOddsHistory.com](http://SportsOddsHistory.com), which uses odds from BetMGM from just before the start of the season.

Stroud, QB, 2nd (+850) Will Anderson, EDGE, 3rd (+400) 2022 Garrett Wilson, WR, 10th (+2000) Sauce Gardner, CB, 4th (+1200) 2021 Ja’Marr Chase, WR, 5th (+1800) Micah Parsons, EDGE, 12th (+600) 2020 Justin Herbert, QB, 6th (+3000) Chase Young, EDGE, 2nd (+150) 2019 Kyler Murray, QB, 1st (+150) Nick Bosa, EDGE, 2nd (+700) 2018 Saquon Barkley, RB, 2nd (+155) Darius Leonard, LB, 36th (+3050) 2017 Alvin Kamara, RB, 67th (+5000) Marshon Lattimore, CB, 11th 2016 Dak Prescott, QB, 135th (+900) Joey Bosa, EDGE, 3rd 

The NFL MVP is overwhelmingly dominated by quarterbacks, but the Offensive Rookie of the Year has been more of an equal-opportunity award between the three main skill positions. Running backs have won the award twice in the last 10 seasons, but not since __Saquon Barkley__ and __Alvin Kamara__ did it in back-to-back seasons in 2017-18. Wide receivers have captured the honor three times in the last decade, including three times in the last five years. Quarterbacks have five OROY winners since 2016, including back-to-back winners in __Jayden Daniels__ and __C.J. Stroud__ in 2023-24.

The offensive winner has come from inside the top-10 picks eight times in eight straight seasons. Kamara (2017) and __Dak Prescott__ (2016) each won the OROY after being drafted outside the top 60 picks.

Primary pass rushers have dominated the Defensive Rookie of the Year award with five winners in the last seven years. Linebackers and cornerbacks have each won twice in the last decade. The DROY winner has come from inside the first round in eight of the last 10 years. A pair of linebackers, __Carson Schwesinger__ and __Darius Leonard__, are the lone exceptions in the last decade. Narrowing it down even further, the DROY has come from inside the top 12 picks seven times in the last decade.

The offensive side has had four offensive winners start the season at +1800 odds or longer in the last nine years. Schwesinger was the first DROY with higher than +1200 odds to win in the last seven years.

Bets I Considered
-----------------

#### __{{Fernando Mendoza|QB|LV|26740}}__ (LV) Offensive Rookie of the Year (+400, Bet365).

+ __Why I like Mendoza__: He cleaned up at the college level last season. Mendoza led Indiana, once a laughingstock of Big Ten football, to an undefeated record and a national championship, and he captured the highest individual honor by winning the Heisman Trophy. Mendoza is the only rookie quarterback with a clear runway to start double-digit games this season, and Klint Kubiak will call his plays after orchestrating Seattle’s Super Bowl-winning offense last season.

+ __Why I ultimately passed__: Mendoza will be watching from the sidelines in September if minority owner Tom Brady has as much power as it seems from the outside. Brady called it a “[tragedy](https://www.youtube.com/shorts/zyclRMckosM)” to force rookie quarterbacks to play early in their careers. The Raiders will pay $11.3 million guaranteed to Cousins to mentor Mendoza this season, which is a starter’s salary and makes him the 20th-highest paid QB in average annual value. Mendoza will still get the majority of starts, and Tyler Shough nearly won Rookie of the Year in just 11 starts last season. *__The best strategy, in my opinion, is to look to bet on Mendoza when his odds slip in September when Cousins is starting games__*.

#### __{{Jeremiyah Love|RB|ARI|26768}}__ (Ari) Offensive Rookie of the Year (+325, Caesars).

+ __Why I like Love__: The Cardinals selected Love third overall, making him the first RB selected in the top five since Saquon Barkley went to the Giants at No. 2 in 2018. Barkley edged out Baker Mayfield for OROY by totaling 2000+ scrimmage yards and 15 TDs on 352 touches. Arizona took plenty of heat for using the third overall pick on a running back, and he has the highest total value of a contract at the position. Love figures to see plenty of work immediately since the organization will want to justify the selection. Love came in as Brett Whitefield’s [third-best RB](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/prospect-guide/profiles/rookie/rb#/) in his 11 years of scouting, behind only Christian McCaffrey and Bijan Robinson, and Love is a weapon as a runner and a receiver like CMC and Bijan.
+ __Why I ultimately passed__: Barkley is the last running back to win the OROY eight years ago. Quarterbacks (x4) and wide receivers (x3) have dominated the award since then. Barkley faced no resistance for touches during his rookie season, with Wayne Gallman and Elijhaa Penny combining for 58 carries behind him. The Cardinals don’t have to force-feed Love, especially if they fall out of contention and are looking to lose games late in the season to start their March for Arch (Manning). Arizona handed $8 million in guaranteed money to Allgeier in free agency, and James Conner and Trey Benson remain in the mix for now. Love could also get lost in the shuffle out in the desert because the Cardinals won’t be featured in many standalone TV games.

#### __{{Jordyn Tyson|RB|SEA|26751}}__ (NO) Offensive Rookie of the Year (+750, FanDuel).

+ __Why I like Tyson__: He has the highest ceiling in this year’s WR class if he can stay on the field, and we’re hoping for those high-end, outlier performances when we bet in awards markets. Tyson landed in an up-and-coming offense led by Tyler Shough, who nearly won last season’s Rookie of the Year despite starting just 11 games. The Saints ranked 10th in plays per game (63.2) last year, and Kellen Moore’s offenses have consistently been among the best in pace of play. Moore got the best out of his old-young QB, and Tyson is a significant upgrade at the #2 receiver spot. He’s the clear #2 option behind Chris Olave, but this passing attack could be highly consolidated between Olave and Tyson if the rookie WR proves he’s worthy early in his career.
+ __Why I ultimately passed__: I wanted to bet on Tyson based on his ideal landing spot in New Orleans’ offense, but I don’t see much value at his current odds (I’d want +900 odds or longer to bet on him). Tyson surged up draft boards late in the process because of his ceiling potential, but he was a mid-to-late first-round pick for most of the process because of his significant injury history. He missed time in each of his four college seasons because of knee, collarbone, and hamstring injuries. Tyson never participated in athletic testing at the combine or his pro day because of his latest hamstring issue. He’s also the clear second option for Shough behind Olave, who is coming off a 100-catch campaign and his third 1000-yard season in four tries.

#### __{{Jadarian Price|RB|SEA|26765}}__ (Sea) Offensive Rookie of the Year (+1100, theSCORE Bet).

+ __Why I like Price__: He was projected to be selected on Day 2, and he landed in the dream spot in Seattle with the last pick of the first round. Price backed up Jeremiyah Love and Audric Estime at Notre Dame, but he has a runway to be the lead back for the defending Super Bowl champions, which means he’ll be in the national spotlight quite a bit as a rookie. Kenneth Walker bolted to Kansas City, and Zach Charbonnet may not be ready to play until mid-season after tearing his ACL in mid-January. The Seahawks should remain one of the league’s more run-heavy teams after ranking 27th in pass rate over expectation (-2.8%), finishing third in rushing attempts per game (29.8), and 10th in rushing YPG (123.3).
+ __Why I ultimately passed__: Price never logged more than 120 carries in any of his three seasons at Notre Dame, which makes it difficult to project a massive jump in his workload as he moves to a higher level of competition. The Seahawks used first-round draft capital on Price, but GM John Schneider essentially admitted that they reached to select Jeremiah Love’s backup. Schneider tried to trade down from No. 32 to collect more picks, but he didn’t want to move far enough down where he wouldn’t have a shot to select Price in the second round. Price is the favorite to be the team’s lead back early in the season, but Mike Macdonald’s teams have rotated backs early in his tenure, and Charbonnet will be back to steal work by the middle of the season.

#### __{{K.C. Concepcion|WR|CLE}}__ (Cle) AP NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year 2026-27 (+3000, FanDuel).

\>Risk .2 units to win 6 units. Placed at 4:18 p.m. on April 27.

Concepcion landed in the perfect WR corps to quickly climb the depth chart and earn targets as a rookie. He took a major leap in his final college season in a new offense, which helped him to climb into the first round. Texas A&M used him on the perimeter and on more downfield routes than he did in his first two seasons at North Carolina State. Brett Whitefield [saw](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/prospect-guide/profiles/rookie/wr#/) shades of __Brandon Aiyuk__ in Concepcion because of his dynamic ability after the catch. He needs to beat out the underwhelming __Jerry Jeudy__ to become Cleveland’s #1 WR right away, and he’ll eventually compete with __Harold Fannin__ to be the #1 option in Cleveland’s passing game.

__Zay Flowers__ flourished under __Todd Monken__ in Baltimore, and Monken should use Concepcion like Flowers. Monken will put him in motion and use him to stretch the field, and he’ll also get Concepcion the ball in space to take advantage of his ability with the ball in his hands. He also uses those skills to affect the game as a returner. He captured the Paul Hornung Award last season, which is an award to the most versatile player in college football. He led the SEC in receiving touchdowns (9), and he ranked third nationally in punt return yards (456). We’re betting on an offensive award, but voters could use his return production as a tiebreaker of sorts if he’s in a tight race for the honor. My biggest concern for Concepcion is the quarterback play he’ll receive from __Deshaun Watson__ and __Shedeur Sanders__ next season, but his longer odds more than make up for it.

#### __{{Akheem Mesidor|EDGE|LAC|26900}}__ (LAC) Defensive Rookie of the Year (+1800, Caesars).

\>Risk .3 units to win 5.4 units. Placed at 4:18 p.m. on April 27.

Edge defenders have won the Defensive Rookie of the Year award in five of the last seven seasons, and Mesidor presents some value at the seventh-best odds to win the award. The Chargers needed some pass-rushing help after they lost __Odafe Oweh__ in free agency, and __Khalil Mack__ is entering his age-35 season. The Chargers selected the Miami prospect 22nd overall to make an immediate impact since he enters the league at 25 years old — he’s older than __Will Anderson__, who has 30 sacks in three NFL seasons. Mesidor’s age is the reason why he slipped into the back half of the first round, but it’s also the reason why I like taking a flier on him for this award, since he should be better prepared to play right away.

Mesidor is coming off a 12.5-sack season, which was good for third at the FBS level. His odds would be much shorter if he were drafted a little earlier, and he [would’ve been the 15th overall selection](https://x.com/JamesPalmerTV/status/2047785417420992669?s=20) before the Buccaneers pivoted to select his falling teammate, __Rueben Bain__. *The Athletic’s* Chargers beat writer Daniel Popper [described](https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7232655/2026/04/27/chargers-nfl-draft-depth-chart-akheem-mesidor/) Mesidor as a “physical, violent, and energetic edge rusher ready to make an immediate impact.” He’ll benefit from playing across from Mack early in his career, who still draws plenty of attention from opposing defenses even with retirement looming in the near future. Mesidor will play in some showcase games for a Chargers team that has the fifth-best odds to win the Super Bowl.

full_text:
A player’s final numbers compress the entire year into a single narrative — often an incomplete one. Throughout the season, we see glimpses of a player’s fantasy ceiling or floor, yet those periods are often overlooked in the offseason. If we take a closer look, we can use these splits to weigh upside potential versus downside risk.

In the next article in this series, I analyze the production extremes for ten wide receivers and assess which end of the spectrum each is likely to finish closer to in 2026.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/7730fdc3ebe338cccf6139025561a9dbb44b60f6)

\> Redraft ADP courtesy of [ESPN Fantasy Football](https://fantasy.espn.com/football/livedraftresults) (PPR Scoring) and Dynasty Startup ADP courtesy of [Dynasty Data Lab](https://dynastydatalab.com/adp/startup) (SuperFlex)

### __Drake London__, WR, ATL

\> Redraft ADP: 15.4 (WR7), Dynasty ADP: 23.0 (WR8)

Drake London started and ended the season on low notes — 9.1 FPG (WR50) over his first and last three games — but was dominant in between, averaging 24.5 FPG (WR1) in Weeks 4-11. Can London sustain that ceiling throughout the entire 2026 season?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/0ecb1e5651915a6cb44d6558a0a45b4b405b0ca9)

__Across that 6-game ceiling stretch, London ranked top-3 in every pertinent efficiency and production metric, producing at a league-winning level.__ After [failing to reach](https://x.com/FantasyPtsData/status/1933949810408817046?s=20) 100 receiving yards without the aid of OT in 2024, London did so in five of those six games. Notably, Michael Penix was under center for all five of them, and any improvement in their connection only raises London’s ceiling further — his 74.6% catchable target rate in that span ranked 65th.

London’s floor split demands context — a [shoulder injury](https://x.com/RapSheet/status/1964840701541404790?s=20) in Week 1, a [hip injury](https://x.com/NFL/status/1982471700311576839?s=20) in Week 6, and a [PCL injury](https://x.com/FantasyInjuryT/status/1990958883783774607?s=20) in Week 11 limited his effectiveness and cost him five games. With the Falcons losing Darnell Mooney in free agency (vacating 72 targets) and [speculation](https://x.com/BlueridgeBronc1/status/2043842351055958476?s=20) that Kyle Pitts could be traded (116 potential vacated targets), a fully healthy London should easily earn 150+ targets in 2026 — making him my “dark horse” WR1 overall candidate for next season.

Atlanta underwent a significant leadership transition this offseason — Kevin Stefanski taking over as head coach and Tommy Rees as offensive coordinator — with a quarterback competition between Penix and Tua Tagovailoa set to unfold. The outcome matters less for London than it might for others. Minimal high-end target competition and a profile built on both safety and league-winning upside make London a worthwhile investment regardless.

__Fantasy Outlook__: London will be one of my favorite 2nd round picks with an ADP of 14.6 (WR7) in redraft leagues, given his overall WR1 upside. I’m also a massive investor in his late-round 2 WR8 ADP in dynasty startups as a young WR I want to build my entire team around (24.2 years old).

### __Emeka Egbuka__, WR, TB

\> Redraft ADP: 56.1 (WR21), Dynasty ADP: 34.0 (WR11)

Through the first five weeks of the 2025 season, Baker Mayfield and Emeka Egbuka achieved the league’s best QB-to-WR connection, resulting in Egbuka averaging 20.5 FPG (WR3). The collapse that followed was immediate and brutal, with Egbuka producing only 7.8 FPG (WR69) from Week 6 onward. Whether or not he can reignite that top-tier chemistry with Mayfield is the defining question surrounding Egbuka’s 2026 fantasy outlook.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/65fc10ea590da441f1a6d0119babc28ec9b85a2b)

It’s worth noting that Egbuka’s XFP/G was nearly identical in both splits, and TD production helped fuel Egbuka’s ceiling stretch, even though his efficiency was still impressive — 2.71 YPRR (WR3). And that efficiency was powered by the exceptional rapport between Mayfield and Egbuka, who ranked 1st in passer rating when targeted (145.3) and 9th in catchable target rate at 86.6% (1st among WRs with a 13.0+ yard aDOT). So, how did that connection deteriorate so rapidly, reducing Egbuka to nearly a third of that production over the next 12 games?

The culprit was injuries — Mayfield’s [oblique](https://x.com/ScottBarrettDFB/status/1998176068327424125?s=20) in Week 7 and a low-grade left [shoulder sprain](https://x.com/RapSheet/status/1993083841351762167?s=20) in Week 12. Prior to those injuries, he ranked 3rd in ANY/A (8.10), 7th in catchable throw rate (77.9%), and 1st in deep throw attempt rate (14.4%). Post-injury, those metrics plummeted — 4.88 ANY/A (QB34), 72.7% catchable throw rate (QB28), and 8.9% deep throw rate (QB32). With Egbuka suffering a [hamstring injury](https://x.com/AdamSchefter/status/1977776001490071640?s=20) around the same time, it’s no surprise that his production subsequently fell off a cliff.

 Emeka Egbuka from Week 7 onward 😬: - 70th / 99 in PFF Grade - 51st / 99 in Yards per Route Run - 82nd / 99 Highest Drop Rate - 81st / 99 in Contested Catch Win % (26.3%) I think he can settle back in but its underdiscussed how bad he was for 66% of this season. — Marcus Whitman (@TFG_Football) February 11, 2026 

__Over that 12-game floor stretch, Egbuka was targeted 8 times in the end zone, but failed to convert a single one__. With Mike Evans’ departure vacating 59 targets, including 7 end zone targets, Egbuka rekindling his connection with Mayfield is paramount to restoring his WR1 fantasy ceiling. But the opportunity should certainly be there for him to do so in 2026.

__Fantasy Outlook__: Given the top-5 ceiling we’ve seen Egbuka achieve with a healthy Mayfield, his mid-round 5 WR21 redraft ADP feels like incredible value. I think his poor stretch of play after Week 5 has opened a limited buy window in dynasty formats and made his late-round 3 WR11 startup ADP extremely enticing.

### __Rome Odunze__, WR, CHI

\> Redraft ADP: 77.9 (WR29), Dynasty ADP: 57.0 (WR20)

Rome Odunze opened Year 2 as one of the most productive fantasy receivers — ranking as the WR3 through the first four weeks (19.9 FPG) — before completely falling off, averaging 8.3 FPG (WR55) from Week 5 onward. Is Odunze a legitimate Year 3 breakout candidate or a low-end WR2 at best?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/7b19a73f54f41dc9685c455cc3f2ec72e9f64d96)

Odunze’s ceiling split comes with a caveat — 37.7% of his fantasy production was purely TD-driven. While his connection with Caleb Williams was elite during that stretch — 129.5 passer rating when targeted (WR2) — it completely collapsed from Week 5 onward — 43.6% catch rate (last), 60.0% catchable target rate (last), and 57.0 passer rating when targeted (last). Odunze also led the league in uncatchable air yards per game over that 8-game stretch with 54.1.

Reports in Week 13 confirmed the reason for this decline in production: Odunze had suffered a [stress fracture](https://x.com/DrJesseMorse/status/1997065441244860922?s=20) in his foot as early as Week 7 or 8, which was evident in his inability to separate from that point onward.

+ 0.452 average separation score vs. man coverage in Weeks 1-7 (WR1)

+ 0.038 average separation score vs. man coverage in Weeks 8-13 (WR70)

Odunze’s toughness may be well-documented — he played with a punctured lung and broken ribs in his final college season, missing only a few quarters — but his hands are a concern that is harder to dismiss. Odunze had the 6th-most drops among wide receivers last season, with 9 total (10.2% rate). Encouragingly, [Odunze acknowledged](https://x.com/CHGO_Bears/status/2013322736429400106?s=20) there is room for improvement and growth heading into Year 3.

While Luther Burden and Colston Loveland are getting all the offseason buzz, I think Odunze stands to be the biggest beneficiary of the 144 vacated targets left behind by DJ Moore and Olamide Zaccheaus. This Bears offense hasn’t come close to its ceiling yet, and continued growth under Ben Johnson should set up the perfect environment for a Year 3 Odunze breakout.

__Fantasy Outlook__: With how ADPs have been trending, it’s looking increasingly likely that Odunze will be the cheapest Bears receiver. Give the upside he flashed when healthy, I’ll take that discount every with his mid-round 7 WR29 redraft ADP. I’m a little dumbfounded that he’s also going after Luther Burden in dynasty leagues, with a mid-round 5 WR20 startup ADP.

### __Parker Washington__, WR, JAX

\> Redraft ADP: 104.9 (WR38), Dynasty ADP: 104.0 (WR38)

Parker Washington has quickly become a fantasy community favorite after his strong finish to Year 3 (18.4 FPG in Weeks 15-18). While the target competition in Jacksonville is at an all-time high, Washington could emerge as the clear WR1 in an ascending offense.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/e2413f1d3cf78d60aad42b4e57eca42d0bd8905b)

Washington’s ceiling stretch was truly elite — top-3 efficiency, comparable to Puka Nacua and Jaxon Smith-Njigba. Beyond the league-winning production in that span, Washington also dominated the Jaguars’ receiver room — his 100.0 receiving YPG doubled that of anyone else. Notably, Brian Thomas, Jakobi Meyers, and Brenton Strange were all healthy throughout that four-game stretch.

That end-of-season breakout wasn’t a fluke either. Washington flashed a high-end ceiling across the games he saw a 65.0%+ route share (including the playoffs).

From left to right, the above marks ranked 16th, 12th, 16th, 14th, and 15th among all wide receivers. With reports indicating that Travis Hunter will shift to a larger defensive role, that production is an excellent 2026 baseline for Washington.

Following Hunter’s Week 7 season-ending injury, Washington solidified himself as the team’s primary slot receiver and Lawrence’s favorite target, earning a team-leading 0.23 TPRR over the remainder of the season. The best 4-game stretch of Lawrence’s career coincided with Washington’s breakout in Weeks 15-18: 281.8 passing YPG (QB1), 115.3 passer rating (QB1), and 8.74 ANY/A (QB1). If Washington was a catalyst behind Lawrence's Year 5 QB1 production, the case for heavy investment in 2026 makes itself.

While the analytics make a strong case on their own, Washington’s tape speaks volumes to his continuance of WR1 production.

__Fantasy Outlook__: All signs point toward Washington as one of the best fantasy values of 2026 — a wide receiver with both a high-end floor and an achievable WR1 ceiling. With a round 9 ADP in redraft or dynasty startups, he’s one of the easiest draft-day decisions you can make.

### __Justin Jefferson__, WR, MIN

\> Redraft ADP: 14.0 (WR6), Dynasty ADP: 17.0 (WR6)

Justin Jefferson’s healthy seasons have been historically reliable — fantasy finishes of 6th, 4th, 1st, and 2nd overall. That standard made his 2025 finish as a low-end WR2 (11.9 FPG) all the more surprising. The question heading into 2026: how likely is Jefferson to bounce back to a top-5 finish?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/4c44bca7032e4adf4d39a9d4e14e670e2c613fea)

Jefferson’s struggles last season had one root cause: historically awful quarterback play. JJ McCarthy and Max Brosmer were among the league’s worst two QBs, and it showed in their bottom-tier connection with Jefferson — 56.8% catch rate (WR87), 70.5% catchable target rate (WR85), 9.1% drop rate (WR96), and a 55.6 passer rating when targeted (WR104). Each mark was the lowest of Jefferson’s six-year career, by a wide margin.

Zoom out, and the picture gets even uglier — the Vikings averaged 18.5 PPG and a -1.9% pass rate over expectation (10th-lowest) during Jefferson’s floor stretch versus 27.8 PPG and a 4.6% pass rate over expectation (6th-highest) during his ceiling stretch. Wentz was hardly elite in Jefferson’s 5-game ceiling split — 85.8 passer rating (QB31) and 5.24 ANY/A (QB29) — but Jefferson averaged 16.3 FPG (WR9) regardless. Semi-competent play is all it takes for Jefferson to put up WR1 numbers.

Only two touchdowns on the year (zero during his ceiling stretch) make Jefferson one of the strongest TD regression candidates heading into 2026. The short-lived McCarthy era was an aberration; prior to that, Kevin O’Connell had built a strong track record of elevating quarterback play. It won’t take much for Kyler Murray to play at a level that will allow Jefferson to return to dominance.

__Fantasy Outlook:__ Jefferson is currently being drafted at what I believe to be his fantasy floor with his early-round 2 WR6 redraft ADP. I salivate at the idea of having a late round 1 pick and pairing Jefferson with a top-tier RB. His disappointing 2025 season has also opened a limited buy window in Dynasty, while being discounted in startup dynasty drafts at his mid-round 2 WR6 ADP.

### __Jordan Addison__, WR, MIN

\> Redraft ADP: 119.3 (WR43), Dynasty ADP: 97.0 (WR35)

Justin Jefferson wasn’t alone — Jordan Addison was just as much a victim of the Vikings’ messy quarterback situation in 2025. Like Jefferson, Addison thrived with Wentz under center, averaging 16.0 FPG (WR9) in Weeks 4-8 before the bottom fell out over the following 10 games (7.1 FPG). Which production extreme can we expect from Addison with Kyler Murray in 2026?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/89ae66be3fde33c321077f3687e455d45d322c15)

Saying that Addison lacked chemistry with either JJ McCarthy or Max Brosmer would be an understatement — he had the highest drop rate in the league in Weeks 9-18 (18.2%) alongside a bottom-tier catchable target rate (68.2%). While Jefferson was force-fed over that 10-game span (28.3% target share), Addison was fighting for low-quality scraps with the rest of the Vikings receiving corps (16.6% target share). What kind of improvement could Murray offer in 2026?

Murray’s deep accuracy has been a consistent problem for two straight years. His 2025 marks — 29.5% highly accurate throw rate (Last) and 61.4% catchable throw rate (QB27) on such attempts — both ranked below McCarthy’s. Murray was only slightly better in 2024, posting a 36.8% highly accurate throw rate (QB21) and 63.8% catchable throw rate (QB21), but remained ranked in the bottom half of the league on both counts. Murray’s inability to connect with Addison on deep balls could lead to weekly volatility.

That being said, Addison produced at a WR1 level in Weeks 4-8 with Wentz under center — a QB who was no better than Murray on passes 10+ yards downfield. The most valuable thing Murray can bring to Minnesota isn’t arm talent; it’s consistent competency. Addison is a talented receiver, and if he can stay out of his own way off the field, he can be an ADP outperformer in 2026.

__Fantasy Outlook:__ People might forget that Jalen Nailor’s departure vacates 50 targets, and alongside the addition of Murray, makes Addison an enticing selection with his late- round 10 WR43 redraft ADP. Weekly volatility is always a concern with Addison due to his play style, but he is still offering strong upside at an all-time low price in dynasty with his early-round 9 WR35 startup ADP.

### __Michael Wilson__, WR, ARZ

\> Redraft ADP: 113.6 (WR42), Dynasty ADP: 96.0 (WR34)

Michael Wilson’s Year 3 breakout was unexpected, but his transcendence into a league-winner was something else entirely. Was his dominant stretch of play in Weeks 11-18 (21.2 FPG) indicative of an emerging star, or merely a flash in the pan?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/ab90c9526127f5b3453b2792cda0bb006c4d97d9)

When thrust into the WR1 role while Marvin Harrison was sidelined in the latter half of the season, Wilson went from one of the league’s most inefficient receivers to the most productive. Outside of the injuries to Harrison, the other major factor in Wilson’s massive leap forward was Jacoby Brissett taking over at QB. Therefore, looking at the 5-game split when Wilson lined up alongside a healthy Harrison and Trey McBride with Brissett under center raises concern.

Wilson’s abysmal level of efficiency in this stretch ranked below that of Van Jefferson, Xavier Legette, and Olamide Zaccheaus — a damning indictment of Wilson’s standing among a healthy Cardinals receiving corps. I’d even go so far as to argue that Wilson stole Harrison’s breakout opportunity after the latter was ruled out in Week 11 with appendicitis.

Wilson’s breakout was also built completely on volume — 38.0 Routes/G (WR2) — and the 2026 landscape might look nothing like the one that produced it. It was far easier for Wilson to earn volume from heavy personnel groupings when there were no other wide receivers on the team other than McBride.

### __Tee Higgins__, WR, CIN

\> Redraft ADP: 53.9 (WR19), Dynasty ADP: 70.0 (WR26)

Tee Higgins has flashed a WR1 ceiling many times, but he just can’t seem to hold onto it for an entire season. Despite having a top-15 WR ADP in three of the last four years, he had his first career top-15 fantasy finish in 2025. With that track record, what’s Higgins realistic fantasy ceiling in 2026?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/bb32c68c5f2c76c1186fbd546fdff501b5ec60a0)

In all honesty, we should completely throw out the first five games of the Bengals' 2025 season. Not only was the OL horrendous (14.10% pass rate over expectation), but Jake Browning was completely incompetent under center (75.2 passer rating) — going 0-3 while the team averaged a paltry 12.3 PPG.

Beyond the raw metrics, Higgins’ Weeks 6-18 ceiling stretch was carried by touchdown production — 9 total, with a team-leading 8 end zone targets (62.5% conversion rate). His underlying profile was less impressive, with Higgins operating mostly in Ja’Marr Chase’s shadow — 6.8 Targets/G to Chase’s 12.6. The most important stretch of play to examine is the one following Burrow’s return in Week 13.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/6b6f4aeec2862eb3d914d19331a50361db983ec0)

From left to right, the above marks ranked 24th, 12th, 19th, 17th, 8th, and 6th across the full season. The Burrow-to-Higgins connection was incredible in those 6 games — Higgins scored on all 4 of his end zone targets while seeing an absurdly high 88.9% catchable target rate, resulting in a 142.1 passer rating when targeted (WR2). This type of efficiency on one of the most high-powered offenses in the league makes me optimistic for Higgins 2026 outlook.

__Fantasy Outlook:__ Higgins' career (and ADP) has been defined by these peak stretches of play, but drafters are expecting a solid return on that investment over the course of a full season. Given the tantalizing upside Higgins has flashed, I think he is extremely affordable at his mid-round 5 WR19 redraft ADP, while also being an obvious buy if you’re building a “win-now” team in dynasty startups with his late-round 6 WR26 ADP. He’s also an elite Best Ball selection with his high-end weekly ceiling.

### __Jameson Williams__, WR, DET

\> Redraft ADP: 74.5 (WR26), Dynasty ADP: 78.0 (WR28)

A feast-or-famine nature has defined Jameson Williams’ career, and through the first seven games of 2025, it was all famine (8.3 FPG). Williams rebounded to average 16.2 FPG (WR9) in Weeks 9-18, but every fantasy manager is asking the same question heading into 2026: Is that production sustainable across a full season or only Williams’ periodic ceiling?

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/23596f3f9e01b8eee4f74de168f5f753fa7e2547)

It was abundantly clear that Williams was the odd man out in Weeks 1-7 — ranking 3rd in team target share (14.7%), barely ahead of Jahmyr Gibbs (13.7%), and 6th in TPRR (0.15). With a 16.2-yard aDOT, Williams was deployed as a downfield threat to stretch defenses and open up the run game (-2.4% pass rate over expectation). This worked out fairly well for the Lions, who averaged 29.9 PPG in that span, went 5-3, and had Jared Goff earn the 2nd-highest overall passer rating in the league (116.4).

Two significant changes that occurred in Week 10 reshaped Williams’ role — Dan Campbell took over play-calling duties, and Sam LaPorta suffered a season-ending injury (the latter was likely more impactful on Williams). Detroit also shifted to a more pass-heavy approach (1.3% pass rate over expectation), while Williams ran a shallower route tree (11.4 aDOT) with reduced target competition. This led to Williams’ red zone involvement surging — from just 1 red zone target in Weeks 1-7 to 8 in Weeks 9-18.

Williams 2026 projection gets murky from here. Drew Petzing arrives as offensive coordinator after a league-leading 7.3% pass rate over expectation season in Arizona. Normally, that would be an encouraging sign, but context is critical: that figure was an outlier across his three years in Arizona, where his pass rate over expectation sat at 0.1% in 2024 and -4.5% in 2023. The return of a run-heavy offense with a semi-healthy LaPorta (training camp status is currently up in the air) in the mix narrows Williams’ upside considerably and could increase weekly volatility.

__Fantasy Outlook__: The odds that the Lions lean run-heavy, while Williams operates as the clear WR3 in the passing game, will only fuel further weekly volatility. His early-round 7 WR26 redraft ADP appears affordable, but there are several WRs going after Williams I would much rather draft: Rome Odunze, Marvin Harrison, Christian Watson, or Luther Burden. However, given his age (24.2), his mid-round 7 WR28 dynasty ADP is still enticing.

### __Quentin Johnston__, WR, LAC

\> Redraft ADP: 129.8 (WR49), Dynasty ADP: 130.0 (WR50)

Johnston opened and closed Year 3 on fire, averaging 19.1 FPG (WR4) across his first four and last two games. The stretch in between was an entirely different story: two scoreless performances leading to an average of 7.2 FPG (WR65). This boom-or-bust profile isn’t new for Johnston, and the question heading into 2026 is whether it ever smooths out.

![](STATIC_ASSET_URI/photos/9b83a1dbc288602fb021559de1312f5d9640f141/54dd5533f7d230e53bede435c83d19454c67c7fb)

It's no coincidence that Johnston’s Weeks 5-14 collapse aligned with McConkey’s production surge — something I touched on in a [recent article](https://www.fantasypoints.com/nfl/articles/2026/dynasty-buys-and-sells-march#/). The primary driver of Johnston’s steep decline in production was Joe Alt’s injury in Week 4, forcing a fundamental shift in how the Chargers offense operated. It was essentially a death sentence for a deep-threat X receiver like Johnston.

Johnston’s strong finish in Weeks 16-17 (17.6 FPG) coincided with the return to his normal role (22.3 aDOT), which was a far cry from how he was deployed in Weeks 5-14 (8.9 aDOT). That dramatic shift extended beyond Johnston individually, with the Chargers’ pass rate over expectation falling from a league-leading 10.1% in Weeks 1-4 to just 1.4% in Weeks 5-14. Johnston’s upside appears tied to the offensive line and how he’s utilized schematically.

Good news: the 2026 outlook for the Chargers’ OL is promising — Alt and Rashawn Slater (presumably) return healthy, with Tyler Biadasz adding an upgrade at center via free agency. Plus, the hiring of Mike McDaniel as offensive coordinator further strengthens the case for this offense taking a leap forward. But the elephant in the room is Johnston’s worsening drop rate — a three-year progression of 4.5%, 8.0%, and 10.1% in 2025.

Still, Johnston holds a special place in my heart. He’s like that toy your friend played with once, got bored with, and threw aside. I’ll be damned if he goes completely unappreciated, and when this offense ascends in 2026, I won’t be giving Johnston back so easily.

__Fantasy Outlook__: Johnston is a truly polarizing player; some have no faith, and others remain optimistic. With a late-round 11 WR49 redraft ADP, there are very few wide receivers going that late that have demonstrated WR1 upside as often as Johnston has. I feel the same way about Johnston’s dynasty outlook, given the affordability he currently has at a late-round 11 WR50 ADP in startups.
